1:
Henry opens with the difficulty of the chapter itself: quiet and peaceable reigns, though the best to live in, are the worst to write of, yielding least variety of matter for a historian to entertain his reader with. The first question is what Tola delivered Israel from, since no oppression has been mentioned. Gill and Keil answer alike, that the saving was from within. Gill denies that the phrase implies Abimelech had defended anyone, since he was no judge of God's raising up but a usurper who left the people in idolatry, and takes Tola for a happy instrument of composing the dissensions he had caused, recovering them from idolatry and protecting their liberties. Keil states the problem as a problem, refuses the assumption that the Israelites had been constantly harassed by neighbours, and holds that Tola rose as deliverer even supposing he only regulated the affairs of the tribes that acknowledged him and, by keeping the nation from idolatry, guarded it against fresh oppression from without. He limits the jurisdiction too, to the northern and perhaps eastern tribes but not the southern, who had taken no part in the earlier war of freedom nor stood under Abimelech. Clarke reasons from the silence: since Tola held office twenty-three years after those troubles the land is likely to have had rest, no enemy making incursions during his presidency and Jair's, which together ran forty-five years. Ellicott finds a smaller concession in the phrasing, that there arose implies a less direct call than the words used of other judges; and he alone allows Abimelech something, that evil as his rebellions were, he may not improbably have kept foreign enemies in check, though he is not counted among the judges.

On the man himself they diverge over his tribe. Henry calls Issachar a tribe disposed to serve, since he bowed his shoulder to bear, and finds it the more remarkable that one of it is raised to rule, those who humble themselves being exalted; the name signifies a worm, but as it was his ancestor's he was not ashamed of it. Ellicott calls the same tribe indolent, notes that Tola seems the only judge it ever furnished, and suggests that both his name and his father's may be connected with the trade in purple dyes, the word meaning the worm from which the dye was taken. Henry alone explains why a man of Issachar settled in Mount Ephraim — it lay more in the heart of the country, so that people might the more conveniently resort to him for judgment — and reads Jair's Gileadite origin the same practical way, that while the honour of government shifted from tribe to tribe before settling in Judah, God took care that those who lay remote should sometimes share it.

The thirty sons on thirty ass colts are read as office by two and as display by one. Gill takes riding for a mark of honour and supposes the sons were appointed under their father to do justice in the several parts of the country; Clarke agrees they were persons of consideration keeping up a dignity in their departments, and infers prosperity from a man able to give a village to each of thirty sons. Ellicott sees an ostentatious polygamy, and observes that the horse was little used in Palestine till much later, its introduction being always discouraged by the prophets. Both he and Keil hear the pun running through the verse, on the judge's name, the word for ass colts and the word for cities, the last purposely altered for the play; Ellicott adds that such wordplay in serious narrative points to a very early stage of the literature, and that the Greek translators, writing for Gentiles who did not value asses as Palestine did, euphemised the word into foals and so happily kept the play alive with their own word for cities.
5:
On the burial place Gill and Ellicott do the same work from the same sources and reach the same end. Both weigh the Kamon that Eusebius and Jerome put six miles from Megiddo against the city of Gilead named by Josephus and the Kamon that Polybius mentions near Pella, and both decide for Gilead — Gill adding that Jerome's village is simply not the same place, but rather the town Polybius lists among the cities of Peraea taken by Antiochus.

The catalogue of gods that follows is counted two ways. Keil and Ellicott both count seven and both call the count significant, neither appealing to the other. Keil sets the seven deities against the seven nations from whose hands the Lord had delivered Israel, and calls the correspondence unmistakeable, Israel having balanced the tale of deliverances with an equal tale of idols and so filled up the measure of its iniquity; Ellicott calls the symmetry with the seven retributive oppressions obvious. Clarke instead numbers five, pairing each nation with its deity — Syria with Bel, Zidon with Astarte, Moab with Chemosh, Ammon with Milcom, the Philistines with Dagon — and explains that they are called gods in the plural because their images and shrines were multiplied through the land. Ellicott's method here is his own: holding that Milton drew his details from a learned treatise on the Syrian deities, he illustrates the whole list out of Paradise Lost — the Syrian damsels lamenting Thammuz, Astarte with her crescent horns to whose image Sidonian virgins paid their vows, Chemosh the dread of Moab's sons, Moloch worshipped in Rabba, and Dagon shamed on the threshold of his own temple, head and hands lopped off.

Henry alone treats the apostasy as a blunder as well as a sin. It looks, he says, as if the chief trade of Israel had been to import deities from all countries, and it is hard to say whether that was more impious or impolitic. They made themselves mean and despicable by it, since no nation with any sense of honour changed its gods; much of their wealth must have gone out in offerings to the mother temples abroad, and the priests of those deities would follow in crowds and take root, so that strangers devoured their strength. If it was done to ingratiate themselves with their neighbours they were justly disappointed, for the nations they courted became their oppressors, a man being punished in the thing wherein he offends. He notices too that they did not even admit the God of Israel among the many but cast him off entirely: those who think to serve both God and Mammon will soon forsake God, for if God have not all the heart he will soon have none of it. And on the punishment: had they fallen into the hands of the Lord immediately they might have found his mercies great, but he let them fall into the hands of men, whose tender mercies are cruel — the one nation lying south-west and the other north-east, so that between those two millstones they were crushed, which is what the word rendered oppressed actually says.

The date is where the two habits of mind part most cleanly: Ellicott declares the narrative evidently imperfect, since no year is specified. Gill supplies three answers instead: one authority makes it the year Jair died, another the first year of the bondage, and two more read the phrase as from that year, the vexing continuing thenceforward. Ellicott does find a third pun here, the pair of verbs for vexing and oppressing being an assonance like broke and yoke in English; and he glosses the opening clause literally as added to do evil, joining new sins to the old. Clarke settles the geography, the Philistines west of Jordan and the Ammonites east, joined for the occasion though the Ammonites were the more active.
9:
How the answer reached them is the question of the passage, and no two of them stop in the same place. Gill sets out the candidates: a prophet, as two rabbis hold, whom a third takes for Phinehas, though he could not then have been living; or a created angel; or the uncreated one in human form. Clarke leaves it open: by what means the reproofs were conveyed we know not, and it must have been by an angel, a prophet, or some holy man inspired for the occasion. Henry cannot decide between the angel of the earlier chapter and the prophet of the later. Keil rules out both, and does it from the silence: this was not given through an extraordinary manifestation, nor through the medium of a prophet, for either would certainly have been recorded. Ellicott goes further, saying the method is simply not specified and suggesting that a stern experience might itself have spoken to the national conviction with a prophetic voice. One silence yields five treatments, from a list of candidates to the proposal that there was no messenger.

The silence about the Zidonians and Maonites is handled three ways. Henry registers the gap plainly: of their being oppressed by these we read not elsewhere. Gill affirms the fact regardless: the Zidonians were left in the land to distress them, and though no mention of the distress or the deliverance survives, that is not to be questioned. Ellicott turns the gap into a principle: nothing definite is recorded of any deliverance from the Sidonians, but the book's narrative is typical rather than exhaustive. On the Maonites he suspects the text, since the Greek reads Midian and some copies Canaan, the Latin the same and the Arabic Moabites, which makes an early corruption probable; and he runs through the candidates — a Maon in the desert of Judah that cannot be meant, a Beth Meon in Reuben, a Meon in Arabia Petraea — before concluding that if a real disaster lies behind the word, Meon must once have been the capital of a tribe that afterwards dwindled. Keil defends a word rather than doubting one: the particle that specifies the sin more minutely need not be removed, since neither its absence from several manuscripts nor its omission by the Greek, the Syriac and the Latin warrants deletion.

Henry has the confession and the reproof to himself. They own themselves guilty like a malefactor upon the rack and promise reformation like a child under the rod, confessing their omissions first, since in these their sin began, and then their commissions. It was kind, he says, that God took notice of the cry at all; and kinder that when they began to repent he sent a message fit to increase the repentance, and so prepare them for deliverance. The reproof he reduces to one sentence that cuts: you have forsaken me, who brought you out of your troubles, and served gods who brought you into them — thus did they forsake their own mercies for their own delusions. Their folly he puts in the commercial terms he used of the imported deities: they had been at a vast expense to obtain the favour of gods who could not help them when help was most needed. Keil reads the sequel the same way but keeps to the text: the threat had its proper effect, since the people confessed, submitted and prayed, and did not content themselves with promising but actually put the strange gods away; and he hears behind the dismissal the song of Moses, which had foretold that they would be sent to the gods they chose. Gill and Ellicott agree on how the invasion widened: the Ammonites, not content with eighteen years of oppression beyond Jordan, crossed into Canaan to subdue the tribes that lay readiest, long success on the one side emboldening them to attack the other.
13:
The refusal to deliver is retracted within four verses, and two of them explain how without contradiction. Ellicott makes the threat itself conditional, as such threats are elsewhere in Scripture, which the sequel proves. Keil goes at the harder end of the difficulty, that God is said to change his mind at all, and answers that the change in his purpose implies no changeableness in the divine nature, since it concerns only his attitude towards his people, or the manifestation of the divine love to man. On the dismissal that carries the threat they agree without argument: Gill says the summons to the gods they had chosen is not serious but ironical, since it was never in their power to relieve, and Ellicott calls it a bitter reproach, setting beside it the mockery on Carmel and the passage where Wisdom laughs at calamity. Keil hears behind it the older warning that they would be sent to the gods they chose.

The repentance is measured differently by each. Gill takes the putting away of the idols for evidence of the truth of it, showing the confessions and humiliations genuine. Ellicott makes the timing the point, that the moment the sincerity was proved God hears them. Clarke grants everything and then withdraws part of it: the reprehension was kind, pointed and solemn, the repentance deep, and they gave proof of its genuineness by putting away all their idols — but they were ever fickle and uncertain.

What is said of God's grief then divides them by scale. Ellicott glosses it literally, that his soul was shortened. Keil reads it as impatience, that Jehovah could no longer look down upon the misery of Israel and was obliged to help. Clarke takes the same clause as far as it will go: what a proof this is of the philanthropy of God, whose compassions move here on a small scale, but by the same principle that led him to give his Son a sacrifice for the sins of the whole world, since God grieves for the miseries to which his creatures are reduced by their own sins — be astonished, ye heavens, and shout for joy, all ye inhabitants of the earth.

The muster at the end is read closely. All three who touch it notice that the Ammonites were literally cried together: Ellicott gives the literal sense, Clarke supposes criers sent out in different directions to stir up all the enemies of Israel, and Gill, following the same reading, reconstructs the movement — having crossed Jordan and distressed three of the tribes, they were informed by a herald that the Israelites on the further side had risen in defence of their country and liberties, and so came back and crossed the river again. Ellicott and Keil agree on the camp, that Mizpeh, a very common name since it means watch-tower, is here the Mizpeh in Gilead also called Ramoth-Mizpeh, Keil adding a modern site for it. Ellicott has one grammatical scruple left: there is no and in the original between the people and the princes, yet the two cannot stand in apposition, since the word for people is never applied to princes. Clarke closes on what the question at the end of the chapter reveals, that the spirit of patriotism had brought the people out but they had no general to lead them, and that in those ancient times much depended on the onset, a war being generally decided in one battle, so that the first impression required a man skilful, valorous and strong to head the attack — when God purposes to deliver, he will in the course of his providence find out, employ and direct the proper means.
